blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Cox proportional hazards regression models the hazard (recall §14.3) as a baseline hazard multiplied by an exponential function of the predictors:

h(t | x₁, …, xₖ) = h₀(t) × exp(b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + … + bₖxₖ).

The baseline hazard h₀(t), the hazard when every x is 0, is left unspecified.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
The log-rank test compares groups but cannot adjust for several predictors at once, as multiple linear or logistic regression can (recall §12.4 and §13.2.5). Cox regression fills that gap for censored time-to-event data. Each predictor multiplies the hazard by a fixed factor, exp(b). The shape of h₀(t) over time can be anything: rising, falling or irregular. That is why the model is called semi-parametric: the predictor part is a parametric formula, the time part is not.

The coefficients are estimated by maximising a partial likelihood (likelihood recalled from §13.1). At each event time it asks: given that one of the at-risk subjects had the event now, how probable was it to be this one, given everyone’s x values? h₀(t) cancels from that ratio, so it never needs to be estimated (the full theory is beyond this book).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: To model time to CBHI dropout on household income, distance to the nearest facility and receipt of the community education intervention, Cox regression estimates each predictor’s association with the dropout hazard, adjusted for the others, as multiple regression adjusts for confounders of a continuous outcome.

points.html: exp(b) is a hazard ratio (§14.6.1): the multiplicative change in the hazard per one-unit increase in a predictor, others held constant.
The model relies on proportional hazards (§14.6.2): each HR is constant over follow-up. Check it.

Events, not subjects, limit the model. A common convention is at least 10 events per predictor: in simulations, “the value of EPV = 10 seems most prudent” (Peduzzi et al., 1995). As for logistic regression (recall §13.2.4), the rule is a guide; smaller ratios can work, larger ones are safer.

blocks.html: Hazard Ratio

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A hazard ratio (HR) is the ratio of the hazard in one group (or at one predictor level) to that in another. In Cox regression it is HR = exp(b).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Exponentiating a coefficient gives an odds ratio in logistic regression and a rate ratio in Poisson regression (recall §13.2.6 and §13.5). In Cox regression it gives a hazard ratio: how many times higher or lower the instantaneous event rate is in one group than in another, at any moment, among those still event-free, provided proportional hazards holds.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: The §14.7 cohort’s adjusted HR for the intervention is 0.58. Inverted, households without the intervention have 1/0.58 = 1.72 times the dropout hazard of households with it, at any moment during follow-up, holding income and distance constant.

blocks.label: Common Misreading
blocks.html: “HR 0.58 means 42% lower risk of dropout.” It means 42% lower hazard: 1 − 0.58 = 0.42, a statement about the instantaneous rate among households still enrolled. The cumulative risk comparison is a different number. In the cohort, the crude HR is 0.62, a 38% lower hazard. The crude cumulative dropout by 24 months (1 − S(24), §14.4) is 1 − 0.661 = 0.339 with the intervention and 1 − 0.505 = 0.495 without, a risk ratio of 0.339/0.495 = 0.69 (0.686 from unrounded survival), a 31% lower risk. The HR and the risk ratio differ because cumulative risk depends on the baseline hazard as well as on the HR.

points.html: HR = e^b. HR = 1: no difference in hazard; HR > 1: higher hazard (shorter event-free times); HR < 1: lower hazard.

An HR is not a risk ratio. A risk ratio compares cumulative probabilities by a fixed time. A constant HR does not mean the risk ratio, or the risk difference, stays constant over follow-up; those change with the baseline hazard.

blocks.html: Proportional Hazards Assumption

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The proportional hazards (PH) assumption states that the hazard ratio between any two groups or predictor levels is constant over follow-up. The hazards themselves may rise or fall; their ratio may not change.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Cox regression can leave h₀(t) unspecified only because every subject’s hazard is the same curve h₀(t) scaled by a fixed factor. If the intervention helps early but not later, no single factor describes it, and the one HR the model reports is a weighted average of different effects.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Why log(−log S) curves are parallel. The cumulative hazard is H(t) = −log S(t) (the total hazard accumulated from 0 to t). Under PH, H₁(t) = HR × H₀(t). Taking logs:

log H₁(t) = log HR + log H₀(t), that is, log(−log S₁(t)) = log(−log S₀(t)) + log HR.

So plots of log(−log S(t)) against log t for the groups differ by a constant vertical distance, log HR, at every t. Curves that converge, diverge or cross signal non-proportional hazards.

Schoenfeld residuals. At each event time, take the covariate value of the subject who had the event and subtract the average covariate value of the at-risk set, weighted by each member’s fitted hazard. That difference is the Schoenfeld residual. If the HR is constant, the residuals show no trend over time; a trend means the coefficient is drifting. The standard test rescales the residuals and runs “a formal score test for slope=0” against (by default, Kaplan–Meier-transformed) time for each predictor and globally (R survival package documentation, after Grambsch & Therneau, 1994).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: If households without the intervention always have 1.72 times the hazard of those with it, at month 6 and at month 20 alike, PH holds. If the protective effect fades (large early, none by month 20), PH fails, and a single HR averages a strong early effect with no late effect.

blocks.alt: Checking proportional hazards: parallel vs diverging log-cumulative-hazard curves
blocks.caption: Figure 14.3. Schematic PH check: log cumulative hazard, log(−log S(t)), against log(time). Groups A and B run parallel (PH holds); Group C starts next to Group A and diverges from it over time (PH fails). The §14.7 cohort’s version is Figure 14.4b.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(survival)
co <- read.csv("data/cohort_dropout.csv")
fc <- coxph(Surv(time_months, dropout) ~ intervention + income_k +
              distance_km, data = co)
cox.zph(fc)
             chisq df    p
intervention 0.273  1 0.60
income_k     1.602  1 0.21
distance_km  1.596  1 0.21
GLOBAL       3.282  3 0.35

Each row tests whether that predictor’s Schoenfeld residuals trend with time. Intervention p = 0.60, income and distance p = 0.21, global p = 0.35 (3 df): no evidence against proportional hazards. A large p-value does not prove PH (recall §8.1: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence); read it with the plot. plot(cox.zph(fc)) draws the residuals with a smooth line, which should be flat.

points.html: Check graphically with log(−log S(t)) against log t (parallel curves) and formally with the Schoenfeld residual test.
If PH fails: stratify on the offending variable, let its effect vary with time, or report separate HRs for separate periods (§14.6.3).

questions.prompt: A Cox model reports HR = 0.6 for a treatment, but the two groups’ log(−log S) curves clearly diverge over log time, and the Schoenfeld residual test gives p = 0.002 for treatment. What does this mean for the single HR of 0.6?
questions.answer: Proportional hazards is violated: the treatment’s hazard ratio changes over follow-up. HR = 0.6 is a weighted average of different effects at different times (for example, strong early and weak later) and should not be read as applying throughout. Report time-specific HRs (split follow-up into periods), let the treatment’s effect vary with time (a treatment × time interaction), or, if treatment is only a covariate to be controlled for, stratify on it (§14.6.3 shows how).

questions.prompt: A Cox coefficient is b = −0.35 with SE 0.12. Give the HR and its 95% CI, and state the result in hazard language.
questions.answer: HR = e^(−0.35) = 0.70. CI = exp(−0.35 ± 1.96 × 0.12) = exp(−0.35 ± 0.235) = exp(−0.585) to exp(−0.115) = 0.56 to 0.89. The group (or one-unit increase) has a 30% lower hazard of the event at any time during follow-up, among those still event-free, with the data compatible with an 11% to 44% lower hazard. It is not “30% lower risk”.

questions.prompt: Explain why proportional hazards concerns the ratio of hazards between groups, not the hazard level itself.
questions.answer: Cox’s model is h(t) = h₀(t) × exp(bx). The baseline hazard h₀(t) may rise or fall freely over time (dropout climbing as a scheme ages); that is not a violation. What must stay constant is the multiplier exp(b), the ratio between the groups’ hazards at each moment, because the model estimates a single b for the whole follow-up.

blocks.html: Stratified Cox, Time-Varying Covariates and Immortal-Time Bias

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A stratified Cox model fits a separate baseline hazard in each stratum of a variable, with the same HRs for the other predictors across strata. A time-varying covariate is a predictor whose value changes during follow-up, entered in counting-process (start, stop] format so that each subject contributes one row per period with a constant value. Immortal-time bias arises when a stretch of follow-up during which, “because of exposure definition, the outcome under study could not occur” is credited to the exposed group (Suissa, 2008).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Stratification. If a variable violates PH, or you only need to control for it and not estimate its effect, stratify on it (a stratified Cox model). Each stratum gets its own h₀(t), of any shape, so PH need not hold for that variable. The price: no HR for the stratifying variable.

Time-varying covariates. Some exposures start partway through follow-up: an education visit at month 3, a job loss at month 10. Coding them as fixed at baseline uses information from the future. Instead, split each subject’s follow-up at the change: a row for (0, 3] unexposed and a row for (3, 12] exposed. Software builds these “start,stop data sets which have multiple intervals for each subject” (R survival package documentation). A related tool, a time-transform term, lets a coefficient change with time, such as exposure × log(t), which is also a direct test of PH.

Immortal time. If “ever visited” is fixed at baseline, every visited household had to stay enrolled until its visit. Those months before the visit are guaranteed dropout-free and are credited to the visited group. The exposure looks protective even when it does nothing. The bias grows with the length of the immortal period (Suissa, 2008).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A hypothetical CBHI programme visits households at month 3 after enrolment; households that drop out before month 3 are never visited. The programme reaches only some households; 100 are visited. The true dropout rate is 2.0 per 100 household-months in everyone, visited or not, so the visit has no effect.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation (immortal-time bias)
blocks.html:
1. Months 0–3: 600 household-months in total (300 from households later visited, 300 from households never visited). 12 dropouts, all among never-visited households, since a household that drops out cannot be visited later.
  2. After month 3: visited households contribute 900 household-months with 18 dropouts (2.0 per 100); never-visited households contribute 400 household-months with 8 dropouts (2.0 per 100).
  3. Naive analysis (“ever visited” fixed at baseline). Visited: 18 dropouts in 300 + 900 = 1,200 household-months, 1.50 per 100. Never visited: 12 + 8 = 20 dropouts in 300 + 400 = 700 household-months, 2.86 per 100. Rate ratio 1.50/2.86 = 0.53: the visit appears to halve dropout.
  4. Correct analysis (visit as a time-varying covariate). Each visited household’s first 3 months are unexposed time. Exposed: 18 in 900, 2.0 per 100. Unexposed: 20 in 700 + 300 = 1,000, 2.0 per 100. Rate ratio 1.00.

In counting-process format a visited household that drops out at month 8 has two rows:

id tstart tstop visited dropout
H017 0 3 0 0
H017 3 8 1 1

Its first 3 months are counted as unexposed, removing the immortal time.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(survival)
co <- read.csv("data/cohort_dropout.csv")
# above the median distance
co$far <- as.integer(co$distance_km > 5.1)
fs <- coxph(Surv(time_months, dropout) ~ intervention + income_k +
              strata(far), data = co)
round(summary(fs)$conf.int, 2)
ft <- coxph(Surv(time_months, dropout) ~ intervention + income_k +
              distance_km +
              tt(intervention), data = co,
            tt = function(x, t, ...) x * log(t))
round(summary(ft)$coefficients, 3)
             exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
intervention      0.61       1.65      0.42      0.88
income_k          0.95       1.06      0.91      0.99
                   coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)
intervention     -0.484     0.617    0.406 -1.191    0.234
income_k         -0.062     0.940    0.022 -2.854    0.004
distance_km       0.108     1.114    0.027  3.928    0.000
tt(intervention) -0.029     0.972    0.179 -0.161    0.872

The stratified model gives near and far households (split at the 5.1 km median) separate baseline hazards; “separate baseline hazard functions are fit for each strata” (survival package documentation). There is no HR for distance, and the intervention HR is 0.61 (0.42–0.88), close to the 0.58 of the continuous-distance model in §14.7 but coarser, since a two-level split adjusts less finely. In the second model, tt(intervention) lets the intervention’s log-HR change by −0.029 per unit of log(months), p = 0.87: no sign that the effect fades or grows. The intervention row is then the log-HR at t = 1 month (log t = 0), not an overall effect.

points.html: Stratify on a variable that violates PH or that you need to control for but not estimate. You lose its HR.

Any exposure that begins after time zero must be a time-varying covariate. Classifying people by what happens later (“ever treated”, “ever visited”) creates immortal time and a spurious protective effect.
An alternative is a landmark analysis: fix a time (say month 3), keep only those still event-free then, classify exposure by that time, and start the clock there.

questions.prompt: A cohort study reports that TB patients who “ever received” a nutrition kit had 20 deaths in 1,000 person-months, against 30 deaths in 1,000 person-months in those who never did. Kits were given at the end of month 2, and 200 of the kit group’s person-months fell before the kit. Recompute the rates with kit receipt as a time-varying exposure, and the rate ratio before and after.
questions.answer:
Naive: kit 20/1,000 = 2.0 per 100 person-months; no kit 30/1,000 = 3.0 per 100; rate ratio 2.0/3.0 = 0.67.

The 200 pre-kit person-months are immortal time: a patient had to survive to month 2 to receive the kit, so no deaths could fall in them. They are unexposed time. Corrected: kit 20 deaths in 1,000 − 200 = 800 person-months = 2.5 per 100; no kit 30 deaths in 1,000 + 200 = 1,200 person-months = 2.5 per 100; rate ratio 1.00. The apparent 33% reduction was entirely immortal-time bias.

questions.prompt: In the CBHI cohort, you suspect the effect of distance changes over follow-up and you only need to adjust for it. Name a way to do this and what you give up.
questions.answer: Stratify on distance (for example, near vs far, split at the median): a stratified Cox model. Each stratum gets its own baseline hazard, so PH need not hold for distance. You give up an HR for distance, and a categorised distance adjusts less finely than the continuous variable (the intervention HR was 0.61 with a two-level stratum against 0.58 with continuous distance). Alternatively, keep distance in the model with a time-varying coefficient (a distance × time term), which does estimate how its effect changes.
